title: Teaching on Purpose #11: Oracy Prompts
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: In the eleventh entry of his 'Teaching on Purpose' series, Adam Kohlbeck interviews teacher Mel Saunders on using oracy prompts to serve the core purpose of driving hard thinking. He argues that learning happens when new material is connected to existing long-term memory during working-memory processing, but the brain is wired for shortcuts and will commit merely plausible connections to memory — illustrated by Year 6 pupils mistaking a 2:3 ratio for the fraction 2/3 and arriving at a wrong answer that feels right. Oracy prompts — sentence stems and starters such as 'I know this is correct because… and I can prove it with an example like this…' — scaffold pupils' articulation of reasoning, freeing working-memory capacity, exposing disguised compliance, and pairing powerfully with Think-Pair-Share. Kohlbeck is careful to bound the technique: prompts can be adapted (using voice-to-text to avoid a dominant partner) and should be dropped entirely when straightforward retrieval, not sustained hard thinking, is the goal.
points: Learning requires connecting new material to long-term memory during working-memory processing, but the brain seeks shortcuts and will commit any plausible-seeming connection to memory.

A worked example — Year 6 pupils reading a 2:3 ratio as the fraction 2/3 and getting a plausible but wrong answer — shows why teachers must keep thinking sustained long enough to test and disprove initial hypotheses.
Oracy prompts are sentence starters, stems or key phrases that scaffold pupils' articulation of reasoning and help distinguish real understanding from 'disguised compliance.'

Prompts free working-memory capacity (less spent on how to start explaining, more on the understanding itself) and combine especially well with Think-Pair-Share by supporting low-stakes oral rehearsal.
The technique should be adapted (e.g., voice-to-text to avoid a dominant partner) and withheld when the task is straightforward retrieval rather than sustained hard thinking.
quotes: When we want students to learn something, we need them to connect that new learning to knowledge that already exists within long-term memory.
So long as the connection appears to be plausible, students are likely to commit that connection to long-term memory.
Oracy prompts are sentence starters or stems or perhaps key words or phrases that are provided to students to help them articulate their understanding.
This technique can create working memory capacity because students don’t have to spend as many cognitive resources working out how to start their articulation of their thinking.
By providing oracy prompts to students just before the Pair stage, we can help them to orally rehearse in a low-stakes environment
When students are retrieving existing knowledge and can do so without any scaffolding, we risk doing more harm than good by using a prompt.
